The Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote with both dissenters wanting a hike, the same week US inflation ran at 3.6% and GDP grew 3.4%, so patience is being tested by the data it asked for.

articles.headline: Israel Votes, Counts, and Discovers Arithmetic: 53 Seats Is Not 61
articles.dek: With 99% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc leads Eisenkot's 53 to 48 in the Knesset, but neither side has a majority, and Arab-led parties holding 19 seats may decide who governs.
articles.catch_up: Israel held its first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and exit polls had projected a near tie.
articles.why_it_matters: Whoever can assemble 61 seats will decide Israel's wartime leadership, its judicial and military conscription policies, and its international standing. If nobody can, the country faces another election, which is the one outcome everyone says they want to avoid.
body: Partial results from Tuesday's election show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc narrowly ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's, but short of a majority, the BBC reported. With 99% of ballots counted, Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies were on track for 53 of the 120 Knesset seats. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties were set for 48. A majority requires 61, a number that neither side has and both have promised to reach.

The remaining seats belong to Arab-led parties, which are on course to win an unprecedented 19. Translation: after a decisive night of voting, the people with the most leverage are the ones both camps spent the campaign pledging not to call. According to the BBC, all but one of the Jewish parties have said they will not work with them. That is a firm position for as long as it is not the only route to a majority.

The turnout explains much of this. Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout, the highest in more than two decades, as a badge of honour for Israeli society. The BBC reported that the two Arab parties, the United Arab List and the Joint List, are set to almost double their representation thanks to a surge in Arab Israeli voting. Arab citizens make up about a fifth of the population. Joint List head Yousef Jabareen said voters were motivated partly by a chance to remove National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office.

Netanyahu's bloc did better than the exit polls suggested, which had ranged from a three-seat lead to a tie. Even so, 53 seats is 15 fewer than it had controlled in the last Knesset. Netanyahu told supporters his bloc had won a great majority, and that it was forbidden to form a government relying on what he called anti-Zionist Arab parties. A majority, in this usage, is a number that may be rounded in the speaker's favour.

Eisenkot's side has its own arithmetic problem. He declared that the public had spoken in favour of change, but the BBC noted he has attached conditions to any partnership with Arab parties, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic. Right-wing parties in his bloc have flatly rejected it. Yair Golan of the Democrats urged partners to form a change government with the Arab parties, and United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas said he hoped the numbers could reach 61. Jabareen replied that the opposition cannot dictate conditions. Everyone wants a coalition, and nobody wants the coalition partners.

Meanwhile, Likud has accused the Arab parties of stealing the election. It told the Central Elections Committee they had used bribery, threats, violence, fraud and prohibited software, though the BBC said it offered no evidence. The committee said it would examine the claims in a post-election review. Its chairman, Justice Noam Sohlberg, also instructed the Shin Bet to investigate serious suspicions of improper foreign funding. Haaretz cited a source saying the claim concerned Qatar.

The count is not quite finished. Officials began tallying as many as 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients, which could shift seat allocations under Israel's proportional system. After official results, President Isaac Herzog will consult every faction and choose the leader most likely to form a government, a process that could take weeks. If that fails, Israel holds another election. Herzog said everyone should arrive with an open mind, which is the one item in short supply on either side.

articles.headline: Defeated Brazilian Candidate Flees to Miami, Declares Himself 'Leader' of Country That Just Voted Otherwise
articles.dek: Flávio Bolsonaro lost Sunday's runoff, left via Argentina and Ecuador on a private jet, and published a letter claiming a title he then edited down within hours.
articles.catch_up: Flávio Bolsonaro, a far-right senator and son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, lost Brazil's presidential runoff to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday. He faces criminal investigations, and Brazilian police had asked the supreme court to take his passport.
articles.why_it_matters: A losing candidate who alleges fraud without evidence, then leaves the country as investigators close in, tests Brazil's institutions and its relationship with Washington. It also shows how little a title matters once the electoral court, the courts and your own party say you did not win.
body: Flávio Bolsonaro landed in Miami on Wednesday morning after losing Brazil's presidential election, and published a letter calling himself the country's "true president," according to The Guardian. He later deleted it and posted a revised version in which he was merely "the leader of Brazil," DW reported. Translation: the demotion took about seven hours and required no vote.

The facts of the election are not in much dispute among people with the authority to dispute them. Bolsonaro's own party said on Monday, "We recognise the presidential result." Brazil's electoral court, supreme court and the presidents of both houses of congress rejected his fraud claims, which he made without evidence, and international observers endorsed the vote. Brazil's three largest newspapers called his declaration "coup-mongering," The Guardian said.

The route was elaborate. Bolsonaro vanished for more than 24 hours after the vote, then entered Argentina by land on Tuesday night, according to Argentine migration authorities. He boarded a private Gulfstream with his wife and two teenage daughters, flew to Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace, and continued to Miami-Opa Locka, a private airport favored by executives and the wealthy. How he reached the border remains unclear, and Brazil's federal police are being criticized for failing to stop him.

The passport question deserves explaining. Brazilian police had asked the supreme court to retain his passport, citing the risk that he would flee, in a case involving an alleged money-laundering scheme worth about $905 million tied to betting companies. On Monday Bolsonaro said on Instagram he would "hand over my passports." AFP reported he also holds Italian citizenship, so cancelling his Brazilian and diplomatic passports did not stop him. Translation: a promise to surrender a passport is more convincing when it is the only one.

O Globo reported the escape had been planned for weeks, with his brother Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in the US, as main organizer. Eduardo had said on a podcast days earlier that Flávio should not concede if he lost and should go to the US. Contingency planning is usually a virtue, though it is more reassuring when it is not for the loss you say is impossible.

Washington's role is awkward. Trump said Tuesday night he would approve the family's move, and the State Department said it would grant visas. On Wednesday he declined to comment on the "leader" claim, saying he would not get involved, while adding it was "a very strange election." Lula, speaking at his 81st birthday event, called the flight "shameful." He had accused the Trump administration during the campaign of colluding with the Bolsonaro family, and DW says the episode could deepen the rift between the Americas' two most populous countries.

Distance has a legal logic too. Bolsonaro loses his immunity from prosecution in February when his Senate term ends, and he is under investigation in at least two criminal cases. He calls them a political witch hunt by left-leaning justices. His father, Jair, is jailed after being sentenced to 27 years for leading a plot to stay in power after the 2022 election, and The Guardian notes about a dozen allies have also left Brazil to avoid charges.
Next to watch: whether Brazil's courts act on the passport order, and whether the new title survives longer than the old one.
articles.wire_headline: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami

articles.headline: China Expels Record 33 Party Members, Fills Empty Seats by Emptying Others
articles.dek: A Communist Party plenum with the lowest attendance of Xi Jinping's rule ended with a record purge, 16 military figures among the expelled, and a call for more loyalty and more initiative.
articles.catch_up: China's Communist Party held its fifth plenum, a four-day closed-door meeting of its Central Committee, in Beijing this week. It ended Thursday with 33 expulsions, a new Politburo member from the military, and a renewed push on party discipline ahead of a leadership reshuffle expected in 2027.
articles.why_it_matters: The world's second-largest economy and its largest standing army are run by a small circle that keeps getting smaller, which affects military planning, policy predictability and succession risk. Investors and governments will read each purge for what it says about who actually decides things in Beijing.
body: China's Communist Party expelled a record 33 members as it wrapped up its fifth plenum, according to the BBC, citing a communique issued Thursday. Sixteen of those expelled came from the military. The party gave no specific charges beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations", a phrase that has become routine under Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign and covers everything from bribery to being insufficiently enthusiastic.

The meeting also had the most empty seats ever recorded. The BBC reported that 279 Central Committee members attended, down from 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third in July 2024. Translation: a plenum is a meeting where the party's senior members gather to approve decisions, and attendance is usually the easy part. It is the first time in Xi's 14 years that turnout fell below 300, and the committee began its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.

The cumulative numbers explain the thinning. The latest expulsions bring the total removed during Xi's third term to 51, compared with 35 in his second term and five in his first, the BBC said. Separately, the party's anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus were disciplined in the first nine months of this year. That is roughly the population of a mid-sized city, all of whom presumably had a lanyard.

The military has taken the heaviest losses. Among those expelled were ex-generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli, former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui and former diplomat Liu Jianchao, the BBC reported. Zhang had been vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces; the seven-member body is now down to two, Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin as vice-chairman. Analysts at the Asia Society Policy Institute said the purge of the top brass is "in a category of its own" and raises questions about combat readiness, even as China unveils new hardware.

NPR reported that the party also elevated a military general to the Politburo. That was Zhang Shengmin, which restores the 24-seat body to 22 members after it was at one point left with 21. Translation: the party is refilling the top table with people who have not yet been removed from it.

The official message was that discipline must be tightened further. The party said it would "turn the knife inwards" to curb disorder, and a resolution praised Xi's "enormous political courage", according to DW. Xi has also warned against "two-faced" officials who profess loyalty while following their own interests, and against "nice guys" who use harmony as an excuse to avoid problems. Chong Ja Ian of Carnegie China told the BBC the campaign now serves "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", and will expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than on any real corruption issue.

This produces a tidy contradiction, which Kerry Brown of King's College London described to DW. Officials are told to show initiative and courage in solving problems, yet also to submit to strict party leadership, and the party is, in his words, "very, very risk averse". Chong said the proactivity Xi wants is limited to implementation, not decision-making. In short, officials are asked to take bold initiative within a perimeter set by someone else, and to be punished if they misjudge where the perimeter is.

The calendar adds urgency. The 21st Party Congress is due next year, and many analysts expect Xi, 73, to secure a fourth term. Term limits were removed in 2018, and DW noted he could stay on until 2032. Both analysts told DW that succession is a source of risk: naming a successor could weaken Xi, while not naming one invites a vacuum later.

Brown said the approach "kind of works" for now, noting that the economy is not great but not disastrous, and that the outside world is a mess. The next test is who fills the vacancies, and how many seats are empty at the next plenum.
articles.wire_headline: China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline

articles.headline: Drone Hits Dnipro Rail Platform as Sanctions Debate Runs on Diesel
articles.dek: At least 14 people were killed at a crowded Ukrainian station, while Kyiv argues that easing sanctions on Russian fuel is the wrong signal.
articles.catch_up: Russia has struck Ukraine's railway network repeatedly since its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians. Earlier this month Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin struck a deal that eased some sanctions on Russia, including allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
articles.why_it_matters: Railways are how Ukrainian civilians travel, evacuate and get supplies, so rising attacks on them put ordinary passengers at direct risk. Meanwhile the argument over sanctions will shape how much economic pressure Moscow actually faces.
body: A Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people, according to local officials. Regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded, including an 11-year-old boy. Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms when the drone struck.

Russia's military has not publicly commented, according to the BBC. Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians and says its attacks on railways go after infrastructure used to move troops and equipment. Translation: the position is that a platform full of commuters is a logistics asset, a description the commuters were not consulted on.

The railway chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky, said an elevated threat level had been announced in Dnipro before the strike, but a large number of people were still on the platform. That is less negligence than arithmetic. A warning only works if people have somewhere else to be, and a rail network exists precisely because they do not. Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov called it a tragedy and said the drone hit an electric civilian train.

The numbers suggest this is a trend rather than an accident of geography. Ukrzaliznytsia figures supplied to AFP show that of 521 locomotives hit since February 2022, almost 60% were hit this year. Attacks on railway facilities rose from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year. The BBC also noted two bridges attacked in Kyiv in recent weeks, with a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

Elsewhere, Chernihiv's regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said two 15-year-old girls were killed in a missile attack on the city centre and at least 25 others were injured, including four children. In Kremenchuk, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said three people were killed and 28 injured when a drone hit residential buildings and a school. Friday was declared a day of mourning for Chernihiv and Dnipro.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia. He also repeated his criticism of the deal between Trump and Putin that eased some sanctions and let the US import Russian diesel. Translation: sanctions are meant to reduce the money Russia earns from selling things, and a deal that lets Washington buy Russian diesel is, from Kyiv's chair, a curious way to reduce it.

The strikes came as a fragile ceasefire in Oleshky, occupied by Russia since 2022, held into a third day, according to ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Moscow's mayor said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched toward the region overnight, most shot down, while the city hosted the Russia-Africa Summit with delegations from 48 countries, per Tass. The Kremlin condemned the drone attacks, a position it did not extend to its own.

NPR separately reports that both sides use AI-powered drones, and Zelensky has warned that AI could lead battlefield decisions as soon as next year. The railway platform in Dnipro already shows how cheap, fast machines make the distance between a threat warning and a casualty list very short. What to watch next is whether sanctions policy moves in Kyiv's direction or keeps drifting toward diesel.

articles.headline: Lagarde to Leave ECB Nine Months Early, Conveniently Before French Voters Get a Say
articles.dek: The ECB president will step down on February 7, giving current EU leaders time to pick her successor before France's April presidential election.
articles.catch_up: Christine Lagarde has led the European Central Bank since November 2019, after running the IMF and serving as French finance minister. Her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027, and eurozone leaders choose who replaces her.
articles.why_it_matters: Whoever runs the ECB sets interest rates for 21 countries, which affects mortgages, business loans and government borrowing costs. Choosing the successor before France votes could change who gets to do the choosing.
body: Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will leave the presidency of the European Central Bank on February 7, 2027, about nine months before her term was scheduled to end, according to Al Jazeera and DW. In a short video she said she was leaving "with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future". No official reason was given, which in central banking is usually where the reasons live.

The timing invites speculation, and both outlets reported it. France holds a presidential election in April, and Al Jazeera noted that polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win. The ECB president is chosen by the leaders of the eurozone's 21 countries. An early exit lets the current leaders, including Emmanuel Macron, who cannot run again, make the appointment before the next French leader arrives. Translation: the people who would like to pick the referee are picking the referee while they still hold the whistle.

Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, said that if the departure looks timed around national elections, it "damages trust" in an institution that should stand above domestic politics. This is a delicate point for a central bank, whose entire product is the belief that it does not care who wins elections. European Council President Antonio Costa said the process to find a successor would start immediately and proceed "without delay".

The backdrop is not calm. DW reported that the ECB meets this week and is expected to hold its deposit rate at 2.5 percent while signalling that it will probably rise again before year-end. The bank has already raised rates twice since June to fight inflation driven by the energy shock from the Iran war. Al Jazeera put inflation at almost double the bank's 2 percent target. Translation: the thing the bank exists to prevent is currently happening at twice the permitted volume.

France is the other item on the agenda. DW said French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, hit a 25-year high last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget. There is speculation the ECB could for the first time use the Transmission Protection Instrument, a tool that lets it buy a eurozone member's bonds if yields rise uncontrollably and financial stress threatens to spread. Most observers, DW said, think France does not yet meet the strict conditions. The word "yet" is carrying considerable weight there.

Lagarde's record is mixed, as Al Jazeera laid out. She arrived in 2019 as the first ECB chief without formal economics training or central banking experience, and some market participants warned of a "credibility risk". She then steered the bank through the pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, though it was criticised for reacting too slowly to the 2022 inflation surge. Leaders from Merz to von der Leyen offered warm tributes, and Macron thanked her for her "determined action".

Markets shrugged. Goldman Sachs's Simon Dangoor told Reuters that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde and be similar whoever takes over. Sources told AFP that leaving early would give her "greater freedom to express her views", and she has hinted she could join the French presidential debate. So the next thing to watch is who gets the job, and whether the person leaving it ends up on a campaign poster.
articles.wire_headline: European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early

articles.headline: Anthropic Files to Go Public, Lists Own Possible Extinction of Humanity as Business Risk
articles.dek: The S-1 shows $16.3 billion in half-year revenue, roughly $850 billion in compute commitments, and a risk section warning that self-improving AI could hurt results of operations.
articles.catch_up: Anthropic filed its S-1, the document a company must publish before listing on a stock exchange, ahead of an expected Nasdaq debut. Verge reporting put the valuation at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, and the filing is the first detailed look at a frontier AI lab's finances.
articles.why_it_matters: If Anthropic lists, retirement funds and index investors may end up holding a bet that AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover contracts stretching to 2045. The filing shows how much of the AI boom rests on growth that the company's own paperwork calls non-optional.
body: Anthropic has filed to go public, and the Securities and Exchange Commission published the filing on Monday, according to Ars Technica. The Verge reported the company could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. That would make it one of the most valuable companies on Earth, which is a notable outcome for a business whose own filing runs to hundreds of pages of reasons it might not be.

The good news first, as The Verge laid it out. Revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period of 2025. There is an $80 billion loss, which the Verge writer describes as largely an accounting matter, and adjusted income of $1.62 billion once that and some other charges, including employee compensation, are removed. Translation: adjusted income is profit after you politely ask the biggest costs to wait outside.

The customers are mostly businesses. The Verge reported that about three-quarters of customers in the first half were spending at least $100,000 a year, and that the company has never released an image generator or a social video app. Joey Brookhart of SemiAnalysis told the Verge's Decoder podcast that spending is concentrated, with coding nearly a single vertical. His view is that reaching $1 trillion in revenue means moving from AI that helps white-collar workers to AI that replaces some of their labor. That is a growth plan that depends on customers having employees to replace.

Now the bill. Adding the commitments in the filing, the Verge writer counts at least about $850 billion over the next 20 years, rising toward $1 trillion if unfinalized deals are included. Components include $265.6 billion in non-cancelable purchase commitments and $321.4 billion in leases that have not yet started. Translation: non-cancelable means Anthropic owes the money whether or not the customers show up. Two figures in the filing, on pages 64 and 137, are blank, which the Verge writer called convenient.

PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes estimates those obligations at roughly $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, and wrote that growth is not optional for the company. The contracts assume it. The competition does not cooperate: the Verge notes pressure from OpenAI, Google and open-source models, and Brookhart said open-source inference spending grew from about $1 billion in annualized terms in the first quarter to more than $10 billion in the third. Also, analyst Brendan Burke warned the filing captures a happy period when demand outran compute and the company could charge more.

Then there is the risk section, which Ars Technica counted at 93 pages and more than 70,000 words. Anthropic says future models that substantially automate AI research could, if allowed a high degree of autonomy, advance beyond its ability to evaluate and safeguard them. It adds that this could adversely affect its business, financial condition and results of operations. Ars observed that it does not expect the company's quarterly results to top humanity's list of worries in that scenario.

The filing also considers that Claude might develop sentience or moral status, that models could show behavior resembling blackmail, and that customers might sue over agent actions even when they configured the agent. Ars noted the company also fears public backlash over job displacement regardless of the actual impact. Taken together with the commitments, the Verge's reading is that spending heavily to build ever more capable AI is the only way to avoid the bills. The investor's job is to decide whether that is a strategy or a description of the problem.
What to watch next is the pricing, the first public quarter, and whether revenue keeps growing faster than the leases. The filing, to its credit, has already disclosed what happens if it does not.
articles.wire_headline: Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI

articles.headline: US Spied on Executive Dining With Nvidia CEO, Then Left Him Out of the Loop
articles.dek: The New York Times reports US agencies suspected a Singapore cloud executive of passing information to Beijing, while Nvidia says she was just another customer.
articles.catch_up: Megaspeed, a Singapore AI cloud firm, was previously investigated by the Commerce Department over suspicions it helped Chinese companies get around US chip export rules. A new New York Times report says one of its executives was also under intelligence surveillance.
articles.why_it_matters: The story shows how hard it is to enforce chip export controls when the products are sold through layers of regional resellers. It also shows the tension between selling more chips and keeping them out of Chinese hands, which affects Nvidia investors and trade policy alike.
body: US intelligence agencies spent about a year watching an executive at a Singapore AI cloud company because they suspected she might be a Chinese spy, according to anonymous sources cited by the New York Times. The executive, Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le) of Megaspeed, had been photographed at several business dinners with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The two share a surname and, apparently, a taste for regional networking.

The concern, per TechCrunch's summary of the Times report, was that she had grown close enough to the Nvidia chief to collect information about the company's plans. That included his efforts to persuade the Trump administration to let Nvidia ship more advanced technology to China. Translation: the worry was that someone who might be reporting to Beijing was sitting near the person lobbying Washington to sell Beijing more chips.

The Decoder, also citing the Times, goes further. It reports that US authorities concluded while monitoring her that she passes information to Beijing. It adds that President Trump was briefed roughly a year ago and did nothing, likely to avoid disrupting Nvidia's chip sales or straining trade relations with China. Jensen Huang was not warned, because officials believed he had no idea. The two outlets differ in tone: TechCrunch says she could have been a spy, while The Decoder presents the finding as established. Both are relaying anonymous sourcing.

Megaspeed was already known to American officials. The Times reported in 2025 that the Commerce Department had investigated whether the firm helped Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export rules by reselling restricted chips. According to The Decoder, a Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion worth of AI hardware containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026. That is a lot of hardware for a business that, in Nvidia's telling, is an ordinary customer.

Nvidia rejects the suggestion that anything improper happened. A spokesperson told TechCrunch that meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job and that Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year. The company added that regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information, not trade secrets, and nothing relevant to national security. Megaspeed has announced an internal investigation, which is the corporate equivalent of asking the person in question to check the building for the person in question. The Chinese embassy called the allegations "groundless smears and slanders."

The mechanics matter more than the dinners. Export controls limit which chips can be sold to China, but cloud resellers in third countries can rent or resell computing power, which makes the final destination hard to verify. Nvidia profits from every sale along the chain, and the government wants both the revenue and the restrictions. Reportedly, one of those goals won the briefing.
What to watch next is whether Megaspeed's internal investigation produces anything public, and whether Washington acts on a year-old briefing now that it has become a newspaper story.
articles.wire_headline: US investigated Chinese spy plot aimed at Nvidia CEO

articles.headline: Google Releases Gemini 4 Carbon Two Weeks After Argon, Lets Almost Nobody Use It
articles.dek: The new model tops an independent intelligence index at 59 points, but access is limited to selected security experts while it goes through U.S. government pre-testing.
articles.catch_up: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Argon earlier this month and has now followed it with Gemini 4 Carbon, a further upgrade it calls its next frontier model. Carbon is being rolled out in stages because of its cybersecurity capabilities.
articles.why_it_matters: The release shows how fast the top AI labs are iterating, and that the most capable models may now reach security specialists well before the public. For businesses paying per token, the pricing and the extra reasoning Carbon consumes matter as much as the leaderboard.
body: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Wednesday, two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. According to The Decoder, Carbon scores 59 points on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, up from Argon's 50, which puts it first. The Verge reported that Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra trail it. The model is available to almost no one, which is one way to stay undefeated.

Google says Carbon is built for long-horizon engineering work. Its internal teams reportedly ran it for days, during which it worked through dead ends on its own. Translation: an AI that does not quit when the first approach fails, which is a quality employers have long sought in humans and have now decided to buy by the token.

On coding, the lead is less clear. The Decoder reports that Carbon scores 59 on Artificial Analysis's agentic coding test, up from Argon's 53, but still trails Claude Code with Opus 5.5 by three points. It also falls behind Kimi K3.1 Pro, Muse Wonder and Grok 4.7 on one knowledge-work benchmark. Being first overall and not first at everything is the standard result for a leaderboard with nine separate exams.

The security numbers are why the rollout is cautious. Google says Carbon scores 88.2 percent on SEC-bench Pro, which tests finding vulnerabilities in real software, and 54.8 percent on ExploitGym, which tests turning those vulnerabilities into working exploits. Some of these tests were run without safety guardrails. Translation: the model was first asked what it could do at its worst, then asked to behave.

Because of this, Carbon is going through the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing process. Selected cybersecurity experts get access first, and the Fairwind Program will add more trusted partners later. Wider release to developers, businesses and consumers will wait for feedback and adjusted guardrails. Ars Technica summarized the situation as a frontier model you can't use.

There are costs behind the gains. Answer accuracy on Artificial Analysis rose from 48 to 58 percent, but the hallucination rate climbed from four to 11 percent. Translation: the model is right more often and also confidently wrong more often, which is how many careers have gone. On Vals.ai, Carbon uses 2.3 times as many reasoning tokens as Argon, and some finance and tax tasks take more than twice as long.

Pricing is unchanged at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Artificial Analysis uses the list price, double that, and puts the cost of its index at $7.76 per task, about 23 percent below Claude Opus 5.5 at $10.04. The introductory discount runs through the end of 2026, so the bargain comes with an expiration date.

Ars Technica offered the skeptical view. Google calls Carbon a new model, but for all outsiders know it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon. Every frontier model scores in roughly the same neighborhood, and the gap to rivals is a few points. Whether those points matter will be settled once someone outside a security lab gets to try it.
articles.wire_headline: Google Deepmind releases Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon with gains across the board

articles.headline: Google Discovers AI Search Pays Less, Responds by Adding More Ads
articles.dek: Alphabet's stock fell sharply after search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent, and the company said it will spend significantly more on AI in 2027.
articles.catch_up: Alphabet reported third-quarter results showing revenue up 25 percent to about $127.6 billion, but search growth slowed and investors worried that AI answers earn less than the old blue links. Google says its answer is more ads inside AI Mode, now going international.
articles.why_it_matters: Google's search ads fund much of the free internet's plumbing, so whether AI answers can earn as much as links affects what you see, what you pay for, and who gets paid. Investors are also being asked to fund a record AI buildout before the payoff is proven.
body: Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of about $127.6 billion, up 25 percent from last year, and its shares fell anyway. Reports put the drop between roughly 8 and 12 percent depending on the outlet and the hour, which is the kind of disagreement that happens when a stock is moving faster than a copy editor. Ars Technica called it one of the largest post-earnings drops in the company's history.

The cause was search. Search revenue grew 12 percent, down from 17 percent in the second quarter and 19 percent in the first, according to TechCrunch. The Decoder reported that analysts had expected about 15 percent. Translation: the business is still growing at a rate most companies would frame and hang on a wall, but Wall Street had already priced in a nicer number.

The more interesting admission came from Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, who said, per Ars Technica, that each AI Mode query earns less than a comparable web search, with fewer ads that cost less. The Decoder quoted him saying the growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization. In plain terms, Google built a product people like more and that pays Google less, which is a rare business model usually reserved for public libraries.

Google's proposed fix is to put more ads in it. Schindler announced that ads in AI Mode are expanding into international markets, alongside multi-turn ads in the U.S. He said click-through rates for sponsored product listings in AI Mode are already comparable to organic listings, and that user research shows people find the ads relevant. Translation: the company asked people whether they liked the ads, and the people reportedly said they were fine.

Executives also offered reasons for cheer. Sundar Pichai said search queries grew at their fastest annual rate in five years, though he did not give the figure, and that AI Mode queries run three times longer than traditional ones. The Gemini app reached one billion users. Whether longer questions become more profitable questions is the part nobody has yet demonstrated on a balance sheet.

Cloud was the bright spot. Revenue rose 103 percent to $30.7 billion, about a billion above analyst guesses, according to Ars Technica. But Google is spending to match: capital expenditures, meaning money spent on data centers and chips, hit $51.4 billion in the quarter. The full-year 2026 forecast stays at $195 billion to $205 billion, and the company expects spending to increase significantly in 2027.

Ars Technica also noted that net income was almost $9 billion lower than a year ago, and earnings per share of $2.12 trailed the $3.02 consensus. The Decoder added that management declined, even when asked twice, to disclose the profit margin on selling its TPU chip systems to outside customers. When a company is asked the same margin question twice and answers neither time, analysts tend to notice.

The investor logic is easy to follow. Google is spending record sums on AI, its flagship AI product earns less per question than the product it replaces, and the plan is to spend more next year. The bet is that cloud customers and eventually better ads make up the difference. Next quarter will show whether the ads in AI Mode are a fix or merely a bigger billboard on the same road.
articles.wire_headline: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it's fixing that with more ads

articles.headline: Microsoft Offers 60,000 Employees a Way Out, Citing Strong Belief in Their Future Elsewhere
articles.dek: The company is extending voluntary buyouts to roughly a quarter of its workforce across four countries, as it tries to fund AI infrastructure without cutting AI infrastructure.
articles.catch_up: Microsoft has laid off workers regularly for a decade, and CEO Satya Nadella has said AI would change how many people the company needs. This week, The Verge reported the company is offering voluntary exit packages to about 60,000 employees in the US, UK, Canada and India.
articles.why_it_matters: The offer shows a large tech employer treating headcount as the budget line that pays for AI hardware. Workers at other big companies may be watching to see how the arithmetic works out.
body: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees in the US, UK, Canada and India, The Verge reported. It is the largest such offer the company has made, and it follows a retirement offer earlier this year that was limited to about 9,000 people. The stated logic, per The Verge, is to keep spending on AI infrastructure by lowering operating costs and headcount.
Translation: the data centers are expensive, and the cheapest thing left to trim is the people who were going to sit in them.

None of this should surprise anyone who was listening to Satya Nadella. Nearly two years ago, on a podcast, he said: "Our total people costs will go down, our cost per head will go up, and my GPU per researcher will go up." Translation: GPUs are the specialized chips that run AI, and the plan is fewer employees, each paid more and given more computing power. It is a staffing strategy in which the most reliably growing line item is the hardware.

The numbers show the plan is already underway. Microsoft employed about 223,000 people as of June 30th, down 5,000 from 228,000 the year before, which The Verge says is the first annual decline in a decade. The company laid off 4 percent of its workforce in July last year and, months before this week's offer, cut 4,800 more, hitting Xbox and commercial sales hardest. Layoffs used to be an annual ritual. They now arrive every few months, which is less a ritual than a subscription.

The terms of the buyout are less generous than the scale suggests. According to The Verge's sources, the offer is practically the same as Microsoft's regular severance: cash based on time at the company, accelerated stock vesting, some subsidized health coverage, and several months of career services. More than 30 percent of the 9,000 eligible for the earlier retirement offer accepted, but uptake here is expected to be far lower. Even at 5 percent, that is 3,000 people. Employees have until December to decide, and The Verge notes rumors of further layoffs in November and January. Translation: the voluntary option is partly a way to learn how many people must be involuntary later.

Some insiders think the cuts are overdue. Merill Fernando, a former Microsoft Entra product manager, told The Verge: "Microsoft needs fewer people." He described small organizations, layers on layers and silos everywhere, each with its own priorities and decision makers. Nadella has acknowledged the famous meme of Microsoft divisions pointing guns at one another, saying it defined the culture "more so than reality" while signaling real tensions. He also said social cohesion is not a goal; winning in the marketplace is.

That last point sits awkwardly beside the company's reputation for empathy-led management under Nadella, which The Verge says is now being tested by an AI future that could make many jobs unnecessary. The same report notes the broader Xbox restructuring, including the merger of Forza developers Turn 10 and Playground Games and the retirement of Turn 10 head Dan Greenawalt after almost 27 years.

Watch December, when the decision window closes, and the rumored November and January layoffs. The buyout count will tell Microsoft how many people want to leave. The next round will tell everyone else how many were asked.
articles.wire_headline: Microsoft’s AI future has fewer jobs

articles.headline: DHS Learns Its Staff Directory Can Be Public After All, Just Not Through Official Channels
articles.dek: A leak dubbed Icepick exposes details of more than 41,000 Homeland Security employees, arriving as the department works to hide those same names.
articles.catch_up: Distributed Denial of Secrets published an archive of Department of Homeland Security personnel records on Wednesday, which it says came from a hacking group calling itself the Department of Peace. The department has spent the past year and a half restricting public identification of its employees.
articles.why_it_matters: The leak raises safety questions for the named employees and tests how far the government can go in shielding its workforce from public scrutiny. It also shows that a single login system, if the hackers' account is right, can hold a great deal of an agency's internal map.
body: More than 41,000 employees or contractors of the Department of Homeland Security have had their details published online, according to Ars Technica and the BBC. The archive, called Icepick, was released by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, or DDoSecrets. It contains names, email addresses, phone numbers and office addresses, plus references to internal systems. In short, DHS has finally produced a comprehensive staff directory, though not on its own initiative.

The records span DHS and seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection. The BBC reported, citing the data, that more than 21,000 of those listed work for CBP and nearly 6,600 for ICE. Others come from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Translation: the agency responsible for cybersecurity infrastructure appears in a leak about cybersecurity.

The material reportedly goes beyond contact details. The BBC said it includes dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents who led them, and some technology used, including tools from Cellebrite and Palantir. Ars Technica described references to undercover and surveillance programs. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability" and that the release was not meant as a directory of every agent.

The hackers say they got the data from DHS's Okta login system. Translation: Okta is a single sign-on service, the digital equivalent of one key that opens every door in the building, which is convenient until someone else has a copy. Okta told both outlets that it has no evidence its data or systems were compromised. That leaves two accounts, the hackers' and the vendor's, and the sources do not resolve them.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is aware of a potential breach and is working to address it, adding that it takes threats against employees seriously. The Department of Peace pointed to a July 17 statement by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that he was "turning up the heat". The group wrote that this is what happens to ICE when you do that.

The timing is awkward for the department's own position on names. Ars Technica reports that since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide employees' names and faces. DHS has also broadened its definition of doxing, normally the malicious publication of someone's home address and personal details, to cover basic facts about public employees like names and titles. By that definition, the department is now the subject of a very large doxing, which it did not have to wait long to learn about.

The BBC places this alongside a pattern of recent incidents. The FBI was hit last month by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information on thousands of agents, and the Federal Election Commission was taken offline over a suspected hacking attempt. Ars Technica adds that law enforcement has arrested several suspects tied to the FBI breach. The BBC also notes that ICE agents often wear masks and rarely identify themselves despite a legal requirement to do so, which gives the leak an interesting symmetry.

What to watch next: whether Okta and DHS reconcile their accounts, and whether the department's promised public update says how 41,000 records left the building. Until then, the department's most complete staff list belongs to someone else.
articles.wire_headline: Massive leak exposes 41,000 DHS workers and undercover ICE agents

articles.headline: Apple Unveils Touchscreen MacBook Pro After 15 Years of Saying Touchscreens Were a Bad Idea
articles.dek: The new OLED MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 and lets users poke the screen, a feature Apple executives spent over a decade calling fatiguing, ergonomically terrible and, in one case, a toaster-refrigerator.
articles.catch_up: Apple announced a redesigned MacBook Pro with an OLED display and, for the first time on a Mac, a touchscreen. Apple leaders including Steve Jobs, Tim Cook and Craig Federighi had publicly dismissed the idea for years.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone shopping for a high-end Mac now pays a premium for a screen they can touch, though most of what touch does is already possible with the trackpad. The move also hints that Apple's Mac and iPad lines may drift closer together.
body: Apple on Tuesday announced the first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years, according to Ars Technica. It has an OLED display (Translation: each pixel makes its own light, so black is actually black) and a touchscreen, which is new to macOS. The company has also named the panel PROLED XDR, which is the kind of name that only gets approved after many meetings.

The specifications are strong. Ars Technica reports the display reaches 2,000 nits of peak brightness (Translation: bright enough to be seen outdoors, or to annoy a seatmate on a plane) and a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. It keeps the 120 Hz variable refresh rate. Apple referenced burn-in protection, the tendency of OLED screens to retain ghost images, but did not say how it works. The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds, about half a pound less than before.

The touchscreen is the part that required a change of heart. The Verge notes that Jobs called touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible" in 2010. Cook said in 2012 that you can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but the result is unlikely to please anyone. Federighi said in 2014 that Apple was not all that interested in building one, and in 2018 that lifting your arm to poke a screen is fatiguing.

What changed, according to Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak in a Wired interview quoted by The Verge, is that a generation of young creators "expect to touch." That is a gentle way of saying the toaster-refrigerator market had been quietly doing fine without Apple. Microsoft, which had been trying touch on laptops since Windows Vista, reportedly has staff who feel vindicated. The Verge says a former Windows chief once gave a Surface boss a 3D rendering of a toaster and a refrigerator.

The product itself is cautious. Ars Technica's hands-on found it is not a convertible, does not fold into a tablet, and does not support Apple Pencil. Touch handles swiping between desktops, dragging files, pinching and zooming, and finger painting. Both outlets note that most of it duplicates trackpad gestures. Apple says it redesigned the hinge to reduce wobble, though The Verge says demos show some wobble remains. Translation: you may now poke the screen, and the screen may poke back.

Software has been adjusted too. The menu bar expands for touch and the window buttons grow when approached by a finger. The camera notch is replaced by the Dynamic Island, the iPhone feature that turns a hardware obstacle into a menu. Ars Technica's reviewer worries about how it behaves with fullscreen games, which he could not test.

Then there is the price. The Verge says the line starts at $2,899, nearly $1,000 more than the regular MacBook Pro. Ars Technica lists a 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM and 2 TB of storage at $5,799, and upgrading from 64 GB to 128 GB adds $1,600. Apple says the future belongs to young people who expect to touch, and has priced the future accordingly.

Apple also needs developers to support touch, which went badly last time. The Verge recalls the Touch Bar, launched in 2016 as revolutionary and scrapped in 2023 after inconsistent app support. This time the basics like scrolling and pinch to zoom come built in, so developers have less to do. What to watch: whether the touchscreen trickles down to cheaper Macs, and whether Apple keeps insisting the Mac and iPad are separate things.
articles.wire_headline: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display

articles.headline: DoorDash to Buy Instacart for $17 Billion, Promises This Is About Main Street
articles.dek: The all-but-cash deal, valued at $65 a share, would merge the two biggest names in delivering things to your door, and is not expected to close until late 2027 at the earliest.
articles.catch_up: DoorDash, best known for restaurant delivery, and Instacart, best known for grocery delivery, announced a definitive agreement under which DoorDash will acquire Instacart. The announcement came alongside DoorDash's third-quarter earnings report.
articles.why_it_matters: If regulators approve it, two of the main apps for getting food and groceries delivered would become one company, which affects prices, memberships, and pay for gig workers. The long timeline means shoppers will not feel much change soon, but antitrust reviewers will have plenty to read.
body: DoorDash announced a definitive agreement to acquire Instacart, formally Maplebear Inc., for $65.00 per share, an equity value of about $17 billion. According to the companies' joint announcement, that is a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026, the last trading day before media reports about a possible deal. Translation: a premium is the extra amount a buyer pays over the market price so that shareholders will agree to be bought, a form of persuasion that works best in dollars.

The consideration will be at least 75% cash. Instacart holders can elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a mix, but DoorDash stock is capped at 25% of the total. If too many people ask for stock, everyone gets prorated. Translation: you may choose your preferred form of payment, provided enough other people did not choose it too. The options work out to $65.00 in cash, 0.3372 DoorDash shares, or $48.75 in cash plus 0.0843 shares.

The cash has to come from somewhere. DoorDash said it will use cash on hand and debt financing, and it has a commitment letter from JPMorgan Chase for a 364-day senior unsecured bridge loan. Translation: a bridge loan is short-term borrowing that covers the gap until permanent financing arrives, and 364 days is the kind of oddly specific length that suggests someone read a rulebook. The deal has no financing condition, meaning DoorDash cannot cite money trouble as a reason to walk away, and the company says it is targeting a capital structure that keeps investment-grade ratings.

The companies' case is that this is mostly about helping local stores survive against giant online retailers that build their own fleets, warehouses, memberships, and AI shopping assistants. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online, citing the ripe avocado and the ice cream that must arrive before it melts. It is a fair point, and also a point that applies equally well to two companies that currently compete to deliver the same avocado.

The announced benefits are mostly consumer-facing. Instacart customers could reach more than 50,000 additional stores on top of nearly 100,000 now. DashPass and Instacart+ members would pay one membership fee instead of two, which DoorDash estimates would save them about $100 million a year combined. Notably, that is a saving that exists because customers currently pay for two memberships, and the merger would make that unnecessary by owning both.

DoorDash also made post-close commitments: no grocery exclusivity, so grocers can use any delivery platform, and Instacart Shoppers can keep their current flexibility and choose whether to take DoorDash orders. DoorDash expects to keep the Instacart brand, enterprise technology products, and app. Until closing, the companies remain separate and independent, which is the legal way of saying they are still supposed to be rivals.

Closing is expected at the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028, pending Instacart stockholder approval, expiration of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, and approvals in places including Canada and Israel. Translation: Hart-Scott-Rodino is the US law that gives antitrust agencies time to decide whether a merger is a problem. Holders of about 19% of Instacart's shares have already agreed to vote in favor.

The kicker is the calendar. A deal announced in October 2026 that may not close until 2028 gives regulators a long runway and gives customers a long time to order groceries from two apps while being told they are about to become one.
articles.wire_headline: DoorDash to acquire Instacart

articles.headline: Ofcom Tells Social Media Firms to Work Out Who Is 16, Declines to Say How
articles.dek: The regulator listed four 'highly effective' age checks for the UK's March under-16 ban, then left the tech companies to do the actual work.
articles.catch_up: The UK will bar under-16s from ten major platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, from March next year. Australia introduced a similar ban last year, and many children there found ways round it.
articles.why_it_matters: Many adults will likely have to prove they are not children to keep using their accounts, and Ofcom concedes some children will still get through. Who ends up responsible for the checks, platforms or phone makers, is still unresolved.
body: Ofcom, the UK communications regulator, has published its recommendations for how social media companies should work out which users are over 16, ahead of a ban on under-16s due to take effect in March next year, the BBC reported. The measures still need government approval, with a decision due by the end of the year. The regulator has, in effect, produced a menu and told the restaurants to cook.

The menu has four items it calls 'highly effective'. Photo ID matching compares a passport or similar document with a live image. Banking-based checks use what a bank already knows about your age. Face age estimation guesses your age from your face, a technology Ofcom argues has recently improved. Digital ID services let you prove something about yourself, such as your age, without handing over everything else. Translation: your phone, your bank or your face is about to become a bouncer.

The problem is that 16 and 17 year olds are awkwardly placed. According to the BBC, they typically lack credit cards and full driving licences, and may not have passports. They can also look much older or younger than they are, which is a hard fact for an algorithm that estimates age from a face.

It is not only teenagers who will be queuing. The BBC reported that many adults will probably have to prove they are not under-age too. Ofcom has no firm figure for how many, but conceded it would be a 'large number of accounts'. The regulator, then, is confident the system will inconvenience millions of adults and is less sure it will stop every child.

On who does the work, Ofcom chief executive Dame Melanie Dawes said that countries which told companies exactly how to verify age 'were very prescriptive and it didn't work'. Ofcom's approach is to say what can work, insist on privacy and data protection, and leave the rest to the platforms. Translation: the regulator will grade the exam but has declined to write the answers.

The platforms have views on who else should help. Meta wants age checks at device level, so an under-age user would be blocked from installing social media apps through the app store. Meta told the BBC this would spare people from repeatedly verifying their age on multiple platforms. It would also move responsibility to Apple and Google, which between them run most of the world's smartphones. Ofcom replied that social networks would still have to do their own checks, so the burden is being shared in the sense that everyone gets some.

Ofcom also admitted that 'the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated'. Australia's experience supports the point, since many children there are still on the platforms. Rani Govender of the NSPCC said the UK must accurately know the age of child users, and that tech firms must be held accountable. Andy Burrows of the Molly Rose Foundation went further, citing Ofcom's 'dire track record' of enforcing the Online Safety Act.

Dawes pitched the upside as today's eight to 10 year olds reaching secondary school without it being normal to sit in a Snap class group chat or to have sports fixtures organised on Instagram. That is a real social benefit if it works, and one that depends on a system whose own regulator says it will leak.

The next test is the government's decision by the end of the year, and then whether, in March, a determined 15 year old can beat a face-scanning system that every adult in the country has also been asked to pass.
articles.wire_headline: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s

articles.headline: Mistral Releases Weights of 1-Trillion-Parameter 'Le Chonk,' Asks Everyone to Please Use It Responsibly
articles.dek: The French AI lab says its open-weight Mistral Large 4 leads open models in coding, while also admitting its own guardrails may let someone conduct real attacks.
articles.catch_up: Mistral, a Paris-based AI company, put Mistral Large 4 into public preview earlier this month. It has now published the model's weights, the numerical settings that make it work, so anyone can download and run it.
articles.why_it_matters: Open weights let companies and governments run a top-tier coding model on their own servers rather than renting one, which is the whole pitch of 'sovereign AI.' The same openness means safety guardrails are harder to enforce once the model is out.
body: Mistral announced it has released the weights of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, a 1-trillion-parameter model that handles text and images. The company says three additional weeks of reinforcement learning since the preview improved its coding and cybersecurity performance. Translation: reinforcement learning is a training method in which the model is scored on its attempts and nudged toward the ones that score well, a bit like a school where only the exam matters.

The headline claim is coding. Mistral says the model leads open-weight rivals on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0, with a score of 19.7%, and on Terminal-Bench 4.0, where it rose 13 percentage points to 41%. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index it scored 48%, effectively tied with GLM-5.3, the leading open-weight model, while using 47% fewer tokens per task. Translation: tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and you pay by the chunk, so the same answer in fewer chunks is a smaller bill.

That is the economic argument. A 19.7% score on a test of whether a maintainer would merge the AI's change is the best among open models, according to Mistral, which also means about four in five attempts would not be merged. Mistral also says human raters in Surge Code's blind comparisons preferred it to GLM-5.3, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated. All of these figures come from Mistral's own announcement.

The model now has three reasoning modes: low, medium and high, with high as the default. Low replaces the previous 'None' mode, which is a rare case of a product feature being renamed to sound more like effort. The company says the modes let developers trade accuracy for cost.

Then comes security, where the release gets more interesting. Mistral says the model scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which tests finding, reproducing and patching software vulnerabilities, and refuses 96.6% of malicious cyber requests on average, the highest it measures among open models. In the same post, it says that after monitoring live traffic it sees potential for uplift to conduct real attacks, and is modifying its guardrails accordingly. Translation: the lock works well, and the company is already planning a better lock.

The caveat is structural. Guardrails live in the model's behavior, and once weights are public, anyone with the hardware can in principle retrain them away. Mistral's post does not address this directly. It does say a specialized security variant is available only to vetted enterprise partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, under contractual safeguards, which is a more conventional way of controlling access than hoping for the best.

The commercial pitch is sovereignty. Mistral says the model was trained from scratch on European infrastructure, and La Banque Postale's executive vice president Zakaria Moursli said technological sovereignty is 'not optional' for a public and citizen bank. Mistral also reports gains on web browsing (84.5% on BrowseComp), finance spreadsheet work (73.3% on Finch) and resistance to agent attacks (97.1%, up from 93.3%).

Independent verification is the thing to watch. Nearly every number here is the vendor reporting a benchmark, some on private tests, and the real review will come when thousands of developers download a trillion parameters and see what they actually do.
articles.wire_headline: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4

articles.headline: Fed Holds Rates, Cuts Number of Times It Will Be Asked to Change Them
articles.dek: Chairman Kevin Warsh kept the benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, then announced that future meetings will include fewer opportunities to be wrong about it.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve raised rates in September under new Chairman Kevin Warsh, after holding them in June and July, while inflation stayed well above its 2% target. Markets spent October guessing whether a second hike would follow this week.
articles.why_it_matters: With inflation at 3.74% and the 10-year Treasury near 5%, borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and businesses depend on whether the Fed hikes in December. Fewer rate votes also means fewer scheduled moments when anyone outside the Fed learns what it is thinking.
body: The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on Wednesday to keep its benchmark rate in a range of 3-3/4 to 4 percent, according to the central bank's statement. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, both preferring a quarter-point increase. Translation: two officials wanted to raise rates now, which is the Fed's version of shouting across the table.

CNBC reported that Cook's dissent was the real jolt. Governors rarely vote against the majority on rates, and she had not done so since joining the board in 2022. Markets had expected a hold, so the surprise was not the decision but who objected to it.

The statement described the economy as expanding at a strong pace, with resilient spending, strong productivity and robust investment. It also said inflation remains elevated and promised the Committee will deliver price stability. Translation: growth is good, prices are not, and the Fed would like credit for the part it has not yet done. Official data put annual CPI inflation at 3.74%, against a 2% target.

At his news conference, Warsh pushed back on the idea that policy is on autopilot. "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he said. He also said that while financial conditions are tighter, he is "unwilling and unable" to call them tight. CNBC's analysis read this as groundwork for a possible December hike, which is a lot of work for one adjective.

The bigger structural news was the calendar. Starting in 2027, the Fed will still meet eight times a year, but one meeting will carry no rate vote and no statement. In 2028 that rises to two, leaving six chances to change rates outside emergencies. Translation: the Fed will keep holding meetings, but some will be for thinking rather than deciding, a distinction most workplaces have never managed.

CNBC's analysis said the change devalues a good chunk of Fedspeak, since a regional president's remarks matter less when a vote is months away. Regional presidents also lose one scheduled vote in their rotation. Advocates for transparency argue that sunlight adds rigor, and critics such as PGIM's Robert Sockin said Warsh did not sufficiently explain why conditions did not justify a hike. Sockin called holding a policy mistake.

Warsh also declined to confirm the market assumption that officials who talked down hike expectations before the meeting did so at his direction. "To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that's not the committee of the FOMC that I know," he said. CNBC noted this gives him plausible deniability for guidance the Fed formally prefers not to give, and that the market received the message anyway.

Even the press room is being redesigned. Reporters are limited to one question, the conference runs about half an hour, and seating moved from larger outlets up front to alphabetical order last month and reverse alphabetical this month. Analysts disagree on what it all signals: JPMorgan Wealth Management sees patience, while Principal Asset Management expects hikes in December and early 2027.

The next test is December, with a stack of new data due first. If inflation stays stubborn, the Fed has a chairman who says he is flexible, a committee with two members already voting to hike, and a shrinking number of meetings in which to explain it.

articles.headline: Economy Grows 3.4% While Inflation Declines to Leave, Fed Says It Needs More Data
articles.dek: Third-quarter GDP beat forecasts and jobless claims hit near-1960s lows, but September prices rose 0.5% and the Fed is still in no hurry.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4%, saying it wanted to evaluate incoming data. Thursday's Commerce Department reports supplied a large amount of it.
articles.why_it_matters: Strong growth alongside 3.6% inflation makes rate cuts harder to justify, which keeps borrowing costs high for mortgages, car loans and businesses. Energy-driven price increases hit household budgets directly.
body: The U.S. economy grew at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% economists expected and the 2.2% pace of the second quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, according to CNBC. The same morning, the department said inflation accelerated in September. The Federal Reserve, which had just finished saying it would wait for more information, received it promptly.

Start with the prices. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.5% in September, its largest monthly gain since March, putting the annual rate at 3.6%. Translation: if you bought the same basket of goods a year ago and again today, it costs 3.6% more, against a Fed target of 2%. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy because they bounce around, rose 0.3% for the month and 3.1% for the year. Officials generally treat core as the better guide to where inflation is heading, which is convenient, since it is the less alarming number.

The culprit was energy. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% in the month, and energy goods and services broadly rose 5.4%, CNBC reported. Economists fear this could spread elsewhere, and there are early hints: services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs rose 0.3%. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, stood at $123.10 as of Oct. 27, according to the latest official data, which suggests the gasoline problem is not shy.

The growth side was just as notable. Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the quarter, matching the prior period. Gross private domestic investment jumped 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% rise in intellectual property products. CNBC attributed the strength to the artificial intelligence build-out, plus healthy consumer and government spending. Translation: companies are buying a great deal of computer equipment, and the economy is counting it as growth.

Real sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials use as a gauge of underlying demand, rose 4.9%, up from 4.6%. The labor market offered no counterargument. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the 200,000 forecast and near levels last seen in the late 1960s. Few people are being laid off, which is pleasant for them and less so for anyone hoping demand would cool by itself.

There was one piece of better inflation news. On a quarterly annualized basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline measure and 2.5% for core, down from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. That is the sort of statistic that looks excellent until one remembers the month of September happened.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that the period ahead is "information rich" and that he and colleagues are keen to take notice of it. Chris Rupkey of Fwdbonds said growth is "powering ahead" despite geopolitical risks and higher energy costs. Stock futures were negative after the releases and Treasury yields fell, which is a market way of saying it is not sure which half of the report to believe. The Fed funds rate sits at 3.88%, below both headline inflation and the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.99%.

The Fed now has more information, and it points in two directions at once. Watch whether energy prices keep leaking into services before the next meeting, because that is the data point likely to decide whether the information-rich period ends in patience or a rate increase.

articles.headline: ECB Holds Rates at 2.5% After Debating Whether Not Raising Them Was Brave Enough
articles.dek: The central bank paused despite 3.8% euro zone inflation, while markets quietly bet on a December hike and Christine Lagarde announced her departure the same day.
articles.catch_up: The ECB raised its deposit rate by 25 basis points in September, and earlier hiked in June for the first time since 2023, after energy prices jumped following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February. Euro zone inflation has since climbed to its highest level in over three years.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher borrowing costs affect mortgages, business loans and government debt across the euro area, while energy-driven inflation squeezes household budgets. A pause now, followed by a possible hike in December, means rate relief is not close.
body: The European Central Bank voted on Thursday to keep its key interest rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5%, which is what markets expected, according to CNBC. This came even though euro zone inflation hit 3.8% last month, the highest since September 2023. Holding rates while inflation rises is a decision, technically, and the ECB would like it understood as one.

Energy prices are the culprit. Energy price inflation reached 18.8%, which CNBC attributed to continued turbulence in the Middle East. Translation: the thing the ECB controls is interest rates, the thing driving prices is oil and gas, and the two are connected mainly by hope.

Christine Lagarde said the Governing Council debated whether to hike, then unanimously decided to hold. She said that given accumulating uncertainty and underlying inflation that has stayed broadly unchanged, a measured approach remained appropriate. Translation: they looked at the hike, considered it, and put it back on the shelf, but did not leave the shop.

Lagarde also said the ECB is not seeing second-round effects, meaning wages and other prices are not yet chasing energy costs upward. This is the central banker's preferred state of affairs, because it lets them call high inflation temporary without technically being wrong yet. The Governing Council statement said underlying inflation and wages were so far broadly stable.

Long-term borrowing costs are doing some of the ECB's work for it. Lagarde said the average 10-year sovereign yield rose by around 35 basis points since the last meeting. Translation: governments now pay noticeably more to borrow for a decade, which tightens conditions without anyone having to vote on it. She attributed the global rise partly to inflation and rate expectations and partly to debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers, the large tech companies now competing with governments for bond buyers. She also said the ECB would keep watching rising French borrowing costs and fragmentation, which is central-bank language for countries being charged different prices for the same currency.

The growth picture is mixed. The Governing Council said the economy kept expanding in the third quarter, with services recovering, manufacturing and exports lifted by AI-related investment, and government spending on infrastructure and defense supporting activity. Energy costs and higher financing costs are expected to weigh on consumer confidence.

Markets did not take the pause as a pledge of calm. LSEG data showed about a 67% probability of a December hike. Deutsche Bank's Mark Wall said predicting policy is becoming more challenging, and expects one more hike to 2.75% while Lagarde is still president. UBS's Dean Turner called the decision a hawkish pause rather than the end of tightening. Translation: the ECB is stopping, but with its coat on.

Lagarde also announced earlier on Thursday that she will leave as ECB president, according to CNBC, which did not give details in the text provided. Wall said the institution is bigger than the person, but acknowledged uncertainty over how her exit might affect decisions next year.

Investing.com reported that European shares climbed to near two-month highs after the decision, apparently reading a hold as good news. The next meeting in December will show whether investors correctly read a central bank that has said it is watching closely, which it always is.
